findings.claim: Ten exam tips tell students to use period vocabulary “to pick up SPaG marks” / “for SPaG marks” (L1, L2, L3, L4, L6, L7, L8, L9, L10, L11, L12).
findings.truth: The period study carries no SPaG marks. The qualification's 8 SPaG marks sit on Paper 1 (Question 5/6) and Paper 3; Paper 2 is 64 marks of assessed content with none. Every instance is rewritten as advice about precision, not about a mark that does not exist.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, Qualification at a glance (168 marks, of which 8 for SPaG) and Assessment information for Paper 1 (“up to 4 marks in Question 5/6”); Paper 2 assessment information lists no SPaG

findings.claim: All 24 questions worded “Explain two consequences of…” are typed “4 marks — Consequence Question” with the scheme “Award up to 2 marks per consequence, to a maximum of 4”. Two per lesson, in all 12 lessons; six exam tips repeat the 4-mark figure.
findings.truth: On this period study the consequence question is worth 8 marks, 4 for each consequence. Booklet P is 32 marks over four questions: 1(a) and 1(b) on consequence, Question 2 an 8-mark analytical narrative, and Question 3 two importance parts of 8 marks each (4+4+8+16 = 32). A student practising to a 4-mark ceiling writes half the development the question needs.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, Paper 2 assessment overview and Assessment information, “Question and answer booklet P: period study”

findings.claim: L8's exam tip is built around “16-mark Make and Defend a Judgement questions on the conquest of Mexico”.
findings.truth: The period study sets no judgement essay and no 16-mark question. The 16 marks in booklet P are two separate 8-mark importance parts. A 16-mark judgement question belongs to the British depth study (booklet B, Question 3/4) and to the thematic paper, not here. The multi-factor content is kept but redirected into the 8-mark importance answer.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, Assessment information, booklets P and B

findings.claim: L2's source box tells students that “Edexcel students treating Columbus’s journals as sources should weigh content, provenance and context together — the highest band specifically rewards integration of all three”. L3's mark scheme repeats “this is exactly the kind of source-critical move the exam rewards”.
findings.truth: The period study provides no sources and sets no source question. Source and interpretation work sits on Paper 1's historic environment section and Paper 3. The historiographical caution about the Las Casas abstract is sound and is kept; the invented band claim is removed.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, Paper 2 assessment information (all questions target AO1/AO2, four questions, no sources)

findings.claim: Six invented examiner claims: “a critical point that examiners flag again and again” (L5), “examiners specifically flag the lazy answer” (L5), “examiners reward answers that show the parts of the system as LINKED” (L6), “Examiners flag the trap of writing three mini-paragraphs” (L7), “examiners specifically flag answers that read like a chronological list” (L7), “Examiners reward students who weigh several factors” (L8).
findings.truth: None can be sourced to any published report, and the house rule bars invented exam claims. The teaching advice inside each is sound, so each is rewritten as plain guidance.
findings.evidence: checker brief, “Invented exam claims … get removed”

findings.claim: “The Edexcel 2026 specification deliberately uses the verb ‘reached’ … and rewards students who treat Indigenous peoples as actors”, plus “is exactly the analytical move Edexcel rewards” (L3).
findings.truth: There is no 2026 edition; the live specification is Issue 6, June 2024. The substantive point is right — the spec's key topic 2 is headed “Columbus reaches the Americas” and its bullets use “Indigenous peoples” — so only the invented year and the invented reward claim go.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md running footer, “Specification – Issue 6 – June 2024”; option P1 key topic 1 bullets

findings.claim: “he crossed the Pacific in 99 brutal weeks” (L7, Magellan).
findings.truth: 99 days. The fleet left the Strait of Magellan on 28 November 1520 and reached Guam on 6 March 1521 — “three months and twenty days at sea”. 99 weeks would be almost two years and would break the 1519–22 dating used everywhere else in the lesson.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Magellan expedition’

findings.claim: L6 says the Requerimiento told listeners “that the Pope had given Spain the Americas under the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)”.
findings.truth: The Requerimiento cited the papal donation (the Inter caetera grant), not the Treaty of Tordesillas, which was a bilateral treaty between two crowns and conferred nothing on the Pope's behalf. L4 already states this correctly (“the Requerimiento … was based on the papal donation”), so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Requerimiento’ (“made donation of these isles and Tierra-firme to the aforesaid King and Queen”); specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md option P1 key topic 2

findings.claim: The Requerimiento is described as “a long Latin and Spanish document” (L6 content), “read in Spanish or Latin” (L6 flashcard) and “often read in Spanish or Latin at dawn” (L6 mark scheme).
findings.truth: It was written and read in Castilian. The point being made — that it was read to people who could not understand it — survives without the invented Latin.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Requerimiento’ (“read El Requerimiento in Castilian”)

findings.claim: “In 1478 they founded the Spanish Inquisition under Tomás de Torquemada to police the orthodoxy of conversos — Jews and Muslims who had converted to Christianity” (L1 content, one knowledge check stem and one mark scheme).
findings.truth: Two errors. Torquemada was not appointed an inquisitor until 1482 and not Grand Inquisitor until 1483, so he cannot have run a body founded in 1478. And in 1478–90 conversos were Jewish converts; Muslims in Castile were not forcibly converted until after 1500, and those converts were moriscos.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Tomás de Torquemada’ (bull late 1478; inquisitors appointed 1482; Grand Inquisitor 1483)

findings.claim: Twice in L4: Alexander VI “had owed his elevation partly to Spanish votes” / “had owed his elevation in 1492 partly to Spanish votes in the conclave”.
findings.truth: There were no Spanish votes to owe. Borgia was the only Spanish cardinal present at the 1492 conclave, the two absent Spanish cardinals did not attend, and there is no evidence Ferdinand and Isabella backed him. His election turned on promises and payments to Italian cardinals, decisively Ascanio Sforza. The sound half of the claim — that he was Spanish-born and depended on Ferdinand and Isabella in Italian politics — is kept.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘1492 papal conclave’

findings.claim: “navigation schools at Sagres” listed among Portugal's investments in the African route (L4).
findings.truth: Modern historians reject the ‘school of Sagres’ as an eighteenth-century legend: there was no navigation school or observatory at Henry the Navigator's court. The real investments — the Elmina fort and decades of royally funded voyages — make the same point.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Prince Henry the Navigator’ (“modern historians hold this to be a misconception”)

findings.claim: ‘Madrid’ is used as the seat of Spanish government throughout: policy “decided in Madrid and Seville” (L6), “It allowed Madrid to argue” (L6), “ten thousand kilometres from Madrid” and an audiencia “directly answerable to Madrid” (L9 content, key fact, glossary and a flashcard), “The lesson Madrid learned” (L8), “Madrid’s attempt to centralise authority” (L10), “no governor could oversee it from Madrid” and “forced Madrid to repeal” (L11), “orders from Madrid took months to reach Lima” (L12), plus eleven more inside mark schemes, and “for Madrid and Lisbon” (L4).
findings.truth: Madrid was a small town in this period. Philip II made it the seat of the court only in 1561, five years after the option closes. Through 1490–1555 the court was itinerant — Valladolid, Toledo, Granada — and the Council of the Indies travelled with it. Every instance becomes ‘the Crown’, ‘the Spanish crown’, ‘Spain’ or ‘the Spanish court’. One ‘Madrid’ is left untouched: it is a wrong-answer option in an L6 knowledge check about where the Casa de Contratación was founded.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md option P1 period bounds (c1490–c1555); Britannica/Wikipedia, ‘Madrid’ (capital from 1561)

findings.claim: L12 places the Council of the Indies “in Seville” in the content, but “based in Madrid” in a flashcard and “sat in Madrid” in a knowledge-check match card — the unit contradicts itself and both answers are wrong.
findings.truth: The Council of the Indies (1524) sat with the royal court and moved with it; only the Casa de Contratación was fixed in Seville. The content sentence loses ‘in Seville’ and the following sentence gains it, so the Casa is still correctly located.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md option P1 key topic 3 (“the role of the House of Trade and Council of the Indies”); Britannica, ‘Council of the Indies’

findings.claim: Charles V is described as at war “against the Protestant Dutch from the 1560s” (L12).
findings.truth: The Dutch revolt began in 1566–68, ten years after Charles V abdicated in 1556 — the very abdication this lesson uses to close the period. The war was Philip II's.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor’ and ‘Dutch Revolt’; the same lesson dates the abdication to 1556

findings.claim: “The historian J.H. Elliott describes this as the moment Spain ‘Atlanticised’” (L12).
findings.truth: Elliott is a real historian and the underlying point — Spain reorienting from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic — is his, but the quoted coinage cannot be sourced to him. The quotation marks are removed and the claim is stated as a paraphrase.
findings.evidence: checker brief, “historians’ interpretations quoted must be real”

findings.claim: “By Charles V’s abdication in 1556, the Spanish Empire stretched … from Havana to Manila” (L12).
findings.truth: Manila was not founded until 1571 and Spain did not settle the Philippines until Legazpi's expedition of 1565. The parenthesis in the same sentence already admits this, so the main clause is corrected to a claim rather than a possession.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Manila’ and ‘Miguel López de Legazpi’

findings.claim: A mark scheme says Magellan's voyage “gave Spain a permanent foothold in Asia that lasted until 1898” (L7).
findings.truth: Magellan's 1521 landing gave Spain a claim, not a foothold. The occupation dates from Legazpi in 1565. The lesson's own content is careful (“The Spanish claim to the Philippines”), so only the mark scheme is out of step.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Miguel López de Legazpi’

findings.claim: Santiago de Cuba is defined as “founded by Velazquez in 1515 as the first Spanish capital of Cuba” (glossary and the matching in-text definition).
findings.truth: Baracoa, founded by Velázquez on 15 August 1511, was the first Spanish settlement and the first capital of Cuba; Santiago replaced it in 1515. The rest of the definition is right.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Baracoa’

findings.claim: L8 places Montezuma's death inside the escape of 30 June 1520: “They were attacked from all sides. Montezuma was killed …”
findings.truth: Montezuma died on 29 June 1520, the day before La Noche Triste, while still a prisoner in Spanish hands. The dispute over who killed him is real and is kept; the sequencing is not.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Moctezuma II’ (died 29 June 1520; “accounts of how he died … differ”)

findings.claim: “Pizarro sailed from Panama in January 1531 with about 168 men, 62 horses and a handful of cannon” (L10).
findings.truth: 168 men and 62 horses is the force at Cajamarca in November 1532, not the force that left Panama. The third expedition sailed with three ships, about 180 men and 27 horses, and the specification dates the voyage to 1530 — it left on 27 December 1530. The Cajamarca figures the rest of the lesson uses are correct and are kept as a second sentence.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Francisco Pizarro’; specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md option P1 key topic 3, “The voyage of Pizarro (1530)”

findings.claim: Huascar is defined as “defeated and killed by his half-brother Atahualpa just before the Spanish arrival in 1532” (glossary, the in-text definition, and “killed earlier in the civil war” in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Huascar was captured at Quipaipan, not killed there — the lesson's own narrative says “capturing Huascar”. He was killed later on Atahualpa's orders, while Atahualpa was already Pizarro's prisoner and specifically so that Huascar could not outbid him with a larger ransom.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Huáscar’ (“Atahualpa had Huáscar killed so that he was not in a position to offer Pizarro a larger ransom”)

findings.claim: The Peru rising is labelled “The 1546 Rebellion in Peru” (heading, key fact, conclusion and four mark schemes), and the key fact has it forcing the repeal of the inheritance clause.
findings.truth: The rebellion ran from 1544, when Gonzalo Pizarro was proclaimed leader, to his execution in April 1548; 1546 is only the year Núñez Vela was killed. The lesson's own narrative dates the rising to 1544 correctly. The inheritance clause was revoked in October 1545, before that killing — so the causal sentence needed the years restoring.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Gonzalo Pizarro’ and ‘New Laws’; the unit's own glossary already says “partially repealed in 1545–46”

findings.claim: “Two years later, in October 1523, Emperor Charles V appointed Hernan Cortes as Captain-General and Governor of New Spain” (L9).
findings.truth: The appointment decree was signed on 15 October 1522 and took effect in 1523. The year is right and matches the spec's “(1523–28)”; the month belongs to 1522, so it is dropped.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Hernán Cortés’; specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md option P1 key topic 2, “Governor and Captain-General of New Spain (1523–28)”

findings.claim: “Bartolome de las Casas … would later cite Montesinos as the moment that changed his mind” (L6).
findings.truth: Las Casas dated his own change of heart to 1514 and a passage in Ecclesiasticus, as L11 of this unit states correctly. He heard the 1511 sermon and was refused absolution by the Dominicans, but he did not name it as the moment. The influence is kept; the false attribution goes.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Bartolomé de las Casas’; the unit's own L11 content

findings.claim: “a Pinzón lookout sighted the white cliffs” (L3 content) and “A Pinzón lookout sighted land on 12 October 1492” (L2 mark scheme).
findings.truth: The lookout was Rodrigo de Triana, an ordinary sailor aboard the Pinta — not a member of the Pinzón family. L2's own content says it correctly (“a lookout on the Pinta”), so the unit contradicts itself and the mark scheme invites a wrong credit.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Voyages of Christopher Columbus’

findings.claim: “They had no metal tools, no horses, no wheels and no immunity to European diseases” (L3, on the Tainos).
findings.truth: The same lesson has Columbus fixating on Taino gold ornaments two paragraphs earlier. The Tainos worked gold; what they lacked was iron. ‘No metal tools’ flatly contradicts the lesson's own central fact.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md option P1 key topic 1, “the discovery of gold, relations with the Tainos and Caribs”

findings.claim: “How many voyages to the Americas did Columbus make in total? — Four, between 1492 and 1502.”
findings.truth: The fourth voyage ran 1502–04, as the same lesson's content says. The span is 1492 to 1504.
findings.evidence: the unit's own L5 content, “His fourth (1502–04)”

findings.claim: Seven list-shaped flashcards: “Roughly how many men, horses and cannon… — About 500 men, 16 horses and 14 cannon” and “It ignores Tlaxcalan numbers, smallpox, Aztec internal divisions and La Malinche” (L8); “Name three diseases… — Smallpox (1520), measles (1531) and typhus (1545)” (L9); “It ignores the smallpox death of Huayna Capac, the civil war, Indigenous allies and the surprise at Cajamarca” (L10); “Name two key provisions of the 1542 New Laws…” (L11); “Monopoly captured the wealth, encomienda and African labour produced it, missionaries justified it, the Requerimiento legalised force” (L6).
findings.truth: A comma-separated set fails the flashcard validator and teaches recall by list rather than by idea. Each is rebuilt as one question with one idea, keeping the same subject matter and staying inside the 30-word limit with no duplicate answer in the lesson.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard validator limits

findings.claim: “The siege was finally broken when reinforcements arrived from Almagro returning out of Chile and from Manco Inca’s Indigenous enemies switched sides” (L10).
findings.truth: The sentence is ungrammatical and reverses the meaning of its second half: Manco Inca's Indigenous enemies switched sides, they did not send reinforcements. One word changes; the dfn and its data-def are untouched.
findings.evidence: internal reading of the sentence

findings.claim: All twelve narrative questions open “Write an analytical narrative explaining how…”, typed “8 marks — Analytical Narrative”. The paper's own stem is “Write a narrative account analysing…”.
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. (a) Leave it — ‘analytical narrative’ is the specification's own phrase for this question, the marks (8), the two stimulus bullets and the ‘You must also use information of your own’ instruction are all correct, and the house copyright rule bars pasting the board's actual question wording. (b) Change every stem to the paper's wording so students recognise it on the day, at the cost of reproducing a past-paper stem. RECOMMENDATION: leave as written — option (a). The form is right and only the verb differs, and it is the copyright-safe choice. No edit made.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md, Assessment information (“Question 2: this focuses on analytical narrative”); checker brief, copyright distancing
findings.ruling: Leave: spec phrase, correct form and marks.

findings.claim: L8 gives “a Spanish core of around 700 men” at the siege of Tenochtitlan, and L9/L12 rest heavy claims on contested demography: central Mexico falling from “15 to 25 million” in 1519 to “1 to 2 million” by 1600, called “the deadliest collapse in recorded human history”.
findings.truth: Two judgement calls. On the siege, Cortés's own count gives roughly 900 Spaniards (700 foot plus 86 horse and 118 crossbowmen and arquebusiers), so 700 counts the infantry only — defensible but easy to misread. On the demography, the 15–25 million baseline is the high Borah–Cook estimate; Rosenblat's low school puts pre-contact central Mexico nearer 4–5 million, and the superlative is stated as fact rather than as one reading. RECOMMENDATION: leave both, but if Tom wants them tightened, change “around 700 men” to “around 900” and hedge the superlative to “among the deadliest population collapses on record”. No edit made.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Fall of Tenochtitlan’ and ‘Population history of Indigenous peoples of the Americas’
findings.ruling: Superlative hedged in L9; 700-man siege count left (infantry only, defensible).

findings.claim: L1 says Matthew Restall's ‘Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest’ “foregrounds the structural conditions: a militarised population, a commercial rival, and a state ideology of religious unity”.
findings.truth: The book is real and Restall does argue against the exceptional-conquistador story, but it is about the conquest of the Americas, not about the conditions of Spain in 1490, and it says nothing about commercial rivalry with Portugal. Not worth an edit — the contrast with Elliott is fair — but the attribution is loose.
findings.evidence: Restall, ‘Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest’ (2003)

findings.claim: L9 attributes the 1545 Mexican epidemic to typhus.
findings.truth: The 1545 cocoliztli is now often attributed to Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C rather than typhus, on 2018 ancient-DNA work. ‘Typhus’ remains the standard textbook label and no mark turns on it, so it is left.
findings.evidence: Vagene et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution 2018, on the 1545 cocoliztli

findings.claim: L12: Potosí “by 1611, with around 160,000 inhabitants … was as populous as London or Paris”; the arbitristas are called “16th-century Spanish economists”.
findings.truth: The population figure is right, but London was nearer 200,000 and Paris larger still in 1611, so ‘as populous as’ overstates it slightly. The arbitristas belong mainly to c1590–1650; the 16th-century price-revolution analysis is the School of Salamanca's. Neither costs a mark.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Potosí’ and ‘Arbitrista’

findings.claim: Small internal date slips left alone: L2's heading “Six Years of Rejection” over a 1485–1492 span; L7's “The campaign that followed lasted three years” against the 1511–15 dating used elsewhere in the same lesson; L5's Columbus “sailed for home on 4 January 1493 with the Pinta and the Niña” (he left La Navidad in the Niña and the Pinta rejoined on 6 January).
findings.truth: Each is loose rather than wrong enough to cost a mark, and each would need a rewrite larger than the error justifies.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Voyages of Christopher Columbus’ and ‘Spanish conquest of Cuba’

findings.claim: Superlatives stated as fact: the Casa de Contratación as “the world’s first imperial bureaucracy” (L6, twice), Cajamarca as “the most disproportionate military encounter in recorded history” (L10), the empire as “the first global empire in human history” (L12).
findings.truth: All three are rhetorical rather than checkable, and all three are the kind of claim a student may repeat as fact. None is wrong enough to fix and each carries the argument of its lesson, so they stay.
findings.evidence: internal reading

findings.claim: Post-period content taught as context: the flota convoys “by the 1560s” (L6), the mita from 1573 (L11, L12), the Manila Galleon and the Philippines to 1898 (L7, L12), Viceroy Toledo 1569–81 (L11), Cadiz “later, briefly” as the monopoly port (L6, in fact from 1717).
findings.truth: The option closes at c1555. All of this is framed as later consequence rather than as examinable content, and the spec's own key topic 3 does put the silver economy, the slave trade and the government of empire in scope. Left as context; the Cadiz aside is the only inaccurate one and is too small to warrant an edit.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md option P1 key topic 3

summary: All 12 lessons checked; none is clean, because two systematic exam errors run through the whole unit. Every one of the 24 ‘Explain two consequences of…’ questions is tariffed at 4 marks when this period study sets 8, 4 for each consequence (F4), and ten exam tips tell students to earn SPaG marks on a paper that carries none (F1). L8's tip is built around a 16-mark judgement essay this paper never sets (F18), and L2/L3 promise source-question credit in a period study that provides no sources (F3). The worst single factual errors are Magellan crossing the Pacific in ‘99 weeks’ rather than 99 days (F15), the Requerimiento resting on the Treaty of Tordesillas instead of the papal donation (F14), Alexander VI owing his election to Spanish votes that did not exist (F9), Montezuma dying during the escape of 30 June rather than the day before (F17), Huascar killed in the civil war rather than on Atahualpa’s orders during his captivity (F22), and Charles V fighting a Dutch revolt that began a decade after he abdicated (F25). ‘Madrid’ is used as the seat of government throughout a period in which it was a small town (F11, 25 instances). The core narrative — Granada, the Capitulations, Tordesillas, La Navidad, Santo Domingo, Cajamarca, Cuzco, the New Laws, Potosí and La Paz — is otherwise accurate and matches the spec bullets, every knowledge-check answer key is correct, and the historians cited (Elliott, Restall, Townsend, Las Casas) are real.
